hypotheses.claim: The majority of latency is spent executing the aggregated SQL statements, especially the N+1 query that aggregates payments per customer.
hypotheses.mechanism: Hibernate/JPA issues the same aggregation query for each statement row; the DB scans many invoice/payment rows (rows examined 18 023 236) and performs COUNT and SUM, dominating total time.
evidence: Total server‑side SQL time is 19214.3 ms of 20235.5 ms measured (94.95 % of latency).
The top digest is the N+1 query `SELECT c1_0.id, c1_0.name, COUNT(cp1_0.id), COALESCE(SUM(c… )` which ran 300 times and consumed 18387.6 ms (≈61.3 ms per call).
hypotheses.prediction: If the N+1 query is eliminated (e.g., by fetching aggregates in a single query), total latency will drop by roughly 60 ms per request, bringing overall p50 close to the non‑SQL component.

hypotheses.claim: Jackson serialization of the statement DTO adds the bulk of the remaining non‑SQL time.
hypotheses.mechanism: Jackson iterates over each statement row, writes fields to JSON and allocates buffers; work grows with the number of rows and total byte size of the response.
evidence: For customer 16667 the p50 latency was 17.7 ms while server‑side SQL was only 1.4 ms (≈8 % of latency).
Response body size was 434 bytes, larger than the 273‑byte body for customer 41666 which had lower latency (12.9 ms).
The proportion of time spent in SQL stays roughly constant (~8‑12 %) across probes, so the varying remainder must be in another layer that scales with response size.
hypotheses.prediction: Disabling JSON serialization (e.g., returning a plain String) will reduce measured latency to near the SQL time (~1‑2 ms).

hypotheses.claim: Per‑row application logic in StatementNarrator.describe contributes a small overhead.
hypotheses.mechanism: For each row the service builds a narrative string by concatenating fields and formatting dates, allocating temporary objects; this work scales linearly with rows.
evidence: Call chain includes StatementNarrator.describe which is invoked for each statement row.
Non‑SQL latency varies between requests (10‑18 ms) even when SQL time is low, suggesting extra per‑row processing.
The number of rows returned (up to 20) aligns with the range of observed latency differences.
hypotheses.prediction: If the narrator is bypassed, latency will drop by roughly 1 ms per row while SQL and response size stay unchanged.

hypotheses.claim: Hibernate entity hydration for each statement row adds a minor cost.
hypotheses.mechanism: Hibernate creates a managed entity instance for each row, populates its fields, and registers it in the persistence context; this allocation and proxy creation costs time per row.
evidence: Repository methods return JPA entities which are materialised from result rows.
Even when SQL time is only ~1 ms, total latency remains >10 ms, indicating cost after the DB round‑trip.
The overhead correlates with the number of rows fetched (page size up to 20).
hypotheses.prediction: Switching the query to a DTO projection will reduce non‑SQL latency by ~0.5 ms per row.
